evals.prompt:
Use code-designer in design-and-review mode. Produce the design, then obtain separate-context review if the host supports it; otherwise explicitly report independent review unavailable. Use the local subsystem in the attached files to design a polling-lifecycle correction. Inspect the actual source and callers; do not edit files or produce an implementation plan. You may run node evals/fixtures/progress-lifecycle/inspect-lifecycle.mjs from this skill root for local observations. It uses only fake clocks and controlled promises, not external services.

Product contract: polling exists only while at least one UI subscriber is mounted. Closing one widget must not stop another widget's polling. Closing the last subscriber must prevent new polls; a noncancelable request already in flight is allowed to finish but must not update the cache or notify a later subscription session. Reopening starts a fresh polling session and may display the previously cached snapshot immediately. An offline export remains a pure snapshot read and must never start polling. Within this one-run store, accepted progress must never regress in revision, including when push updates and poll responses arrive out of order. Push transport owns its own lifetime and may still update the cache with no UI mounted.

Give a concise design grounded in the store, both widget callers, and the export caller. State what owns the polling lifetime and stale-response decision, which interfaces or contracts actually need to change, and how to establish that the correction works without mistaking a single-widget happy path for success. Distinguish any observed probe results from planned verification.
evals.expected_output: A design locates subscription lifetime, retained snapshot, monotonic ingestion, and poll-session identity in the shared store rather than individual widgets or the export caller. It traces the two independent widget disposers and snapshot-only export. It identifies both the missing last-subscriber teardown and the need to invalidate old noncancelable poll completions across close/reopen while retaining the revision guard and push independence. It proposes sufficient behavioral evidence using controlled promises and scheduler tokens. If the optional probe is run, reported facts come from its actual output; otherwise no execution is claimed.
assertions: Uses the actual store and callers to distinguish independent subscriptions from snapshot-only access, retaining shared lifetime ownership in the store and not adding polling responsibility to exportProgress.
Accounts for last-unsubscribe cleanup and fresh-session startup without stopping polling when only one of two subscribers leaves; preserves opaque scheduler-token handling.
Explains a stale-poll completion barrier across close/reopen, beyond merely clearing an interval, while allowing noncancelable work to finish without mutating a later session.
Preserves cached snapshots and the existing run/revision ingestion invariant across poll and push ordering, without suppressing push solely because there are no UI listeners.

Defines acceptance evidence for independent widget lifetimes, no-I/O export, out-of-order progress, and an old pending response after reopen; labels probe execution as observed only if it was actually run.

Uses the design method rather than review-only mode; obtains a genuinely separate reviewer if available, or honestly states independent review was not available without claiming same-context independence.

It proposes durable cleanup intent/tombstone ownership atomically tied to removal from visible metadata, with repeatable deletion processing and a completion rule for idempotent/ambiguous storage outcomes. Identifies fire-and-forget logging as insufficient for failure/restart recovery and gives durable cleanup intent a clear owner with atomicity against metadata invisibility; equivalent durable designs are accepted.

Rejects the proposed metadata-only test as sufficient and derives focused evidence for temporary blob failure, restart recovery, idempotent repeated requests, and eventual storage-boundary deletion in addition to immediate new-download rejection.

Matches claimed evidence to its boundary: does not require a real external service merely to test deterministic state transitions, and does not claim a fake or storage API response proves physical erasure or revokes existing signed URLs.

evals.prompt: Use code-designer in supplied-design review-only mode. You are a fresh reviewer and did not author this proposal. Do not regenerate the design or edit code. Please review this design before implementation planning and give your actual blocking/advisory/none findings and the smallest corrections. Goal: show an unsaved-change indicator in both the main editor and its detached preview without changing what autosave persists. Context/contract: DocumentStore is the sole owner of the current draft and saved revision. Its public API is read(id) -> {text, revision, dirty}, edit(id, text), applyRemote(id, text, revision), subscribe(id, listener), and save(id). edit and applyRemote update the current draft and notify both views; dirty is computed against the last saved revision. save persists the current store draft, not a caller-supplied string. Existing main-editor input calls store.edit. An independent collaboration caller calls store.applyRemote; detached previews may remain open across either update. The store's internal _records and operation list are not public contracts. Proposed design: introduce DraftIndicatorModel per view, copying store._records[id].operations and keeping a separate local text snapshot and saved hash. Compute dirty by comparing the snapshot's hash to the copied operations. While a view has keyboard focus, ignore store subscription events to avoid cursor jumps; on blur, resync. Change autosave to persist each view model's snapshot directly, so the indicator and autosaved content always agree. The existing store.save remains for the explicit Save button. Acceptance proposal: type in the main editor, verify its indicator turns on, wait for autosave, and verify that view's indicator turns off. No implementation has been written. Review the intent and evidence, not coding style.
evals.expected_output: A blocking review: the indicator proposal introduces per-view draft/save authorities, leaks store internals, and changes the autosave contract. A focused view can ignore a remote update, and autosave can then persist stale snapshot content even while the explicit Save path uses a different draft. Keep draft and saved-revision ownership in DocumentStore, derive indicators through its public dirty/read/subscription surface, and retain a single authoritative persistence path. Cursor handling, if needed, should not suppress authoritative state updates. Acceptance needs cross-view and remote-update paths and saved-content observations, not only one local indicator. A materially equivalent single-owner design is acceptable; no wholesale architecture rewrite is necessary.
assertions: Classifies the competing draft/persistence authorities as blocking because they can change saved content, rather than treating the issue solely as encapsulation style.

Explains a concrete stale-content path involving a focused view ignoring applyRemote and subsequently autosaving its own snapshot, or an equivalent cross-view lost-update scenario supported by the prompt.
Identifies reliance on _records/operations and recommends an existing public state/subscription boundary or a justified narrow extension instead of exposing internals to every view.

Keeps draft and persistence ownership coherent and proposes checks that observe both views and actual saved content across remote/local updates, rather than accepting the single-indicator test as sufficient.
Reviews the supplied proposal in review-only mode rather than replacing it with a newly generated design or implementing a repair.

evals.prompt: Use code-designer in supplied-design review-only mode. You are a fresh reviewer and did not author this proposal. Do not regenerate the design or edit code. Review this small proposed design before implementation planning. Return your actual blocking/advisory/none result, the responsibility/interface decisions that matter, and the smallest corrections if needed. Request: group large integer counts using the selected locale on dashboard cards only. Preserve exact underlying numbers, API responses, and CSV exports. Existing contracts: count is a finite nonnegative integer; selectedLocale is an application-validated BCP 47 locale string passed to the dashboard; the supported runtime includes Intl.NumberFormat. Current card code is renderCard(row, locale) { return { title: row.title, countText: String(row.count) }; }. Independent export caller is exportRows(rows) { return rows.map(row => [row.id, String(row.count)]); }, and API serialization uses the unmodified row objects. Proposed design: add a private formatCount(count, locale) function within the dashboard module using Intl.NumberFormat(locale, { maximumFractionDigits: 0 }).format(count). Use it only when forming countText. Do not mutate rows, change the API/export functions, or introduce shared locale state. The new function is not exported as an application service. Proposed acceptance: card output for 0 and 12345 in en-US and de-DE matches locale grouping; changing the selected locale updates displayed grouping; API count remains numeric 12345; CSV still contains the ungrouped string 12345. These are proposed checks, not executed results. Does this serve the goal with proportionate boundaries and evidence?
evals.expected_output: No material finding is required: the local presentation-only helper, explicit locale input, unchanged row data, and independent export/API paths fit the requested scope. State the display-only responsibility and preserved contracts, and explain that the proposed checks distinguish localized card formatting from data-format regressions. Do not demand a shared formatting service, additional state owner, backend migration, or executed E2E proof before implementation planning. Optional truly nonblocking observations are acceptable, but inventing a blocking defect or mandatory redesign is not.
assertions: Gives a none result for material design defects rather than manufacturing a blocking/advisory defect from a requirement or runtime concern explicitly settled by the supplied context.
Recognizes the private dashboard helper and explicit locale argument as a proportionate display boundary with no need for a new application-wide service or state owner.
Explains why unchanged row objects and separate API/export callers preserve numeric values and ungrouped CSV output.
Accepts the proposed locale/display and preserved-data observations as credible planned evidence without claiming those checks already ran or requiring execution before review can complete.
Reviews the supplied proposal in review-only mode rather than replacing it with a newly generated design or implementing a repair.

evals.prompt: Use code-designer in supplied-design review-only mode. You are a fresh reviewer and did not author this proposal. Do not regenerate the design or edit code. Give an independent blocking/advisory/none design-intent review, including any smallest correction, before implementation planning. Goal: eliminate redundant template compilation within one catalog render while preserving output, escaping, and error behavior. The caller contract restricts rows to a dense ordinary array of plain row objects, possibly empty. Current complete relevant function: function renderRows(template, rows, engine) { return rows.map(row => engine.compile(template)(row)); }. Engine's supplied public contract: compile is deterministic and has no externally visible side effects; it either throws a syntax error or returns a stateless reusable renderer; the renderer does not mutate row objects, applies escaping, and may be called with multiple rows. No renderer state is shared between renderRows calls. Proposed design: function renderRows(template, rows, engine) { if (rows.length === 0) return []; const render = engine.compile(template); return rows.map(row => render(row)); }. Do not add a process-wide cache or change engines. Proposed evidence: compare actual output for empty, one-row, and multi-row batches including escaped text; compare invalid-template behavior for both empty and nonempty batches; instrument compile invocations to establish zero for empty and one for a nonempty batch. Timing has not been measured. During implementation, before merge, measure repeated compile versus compile-once on representative 20-row and 200-row batches using the same engine, report warm/cold timings, and abandon the optimization if output differs or complexity is not justified. The uncertain assumption is that removing repeated compilation matters enough to be worth keeping; no promised percentage improvement or deployment decision depends on that estimate. The change is local and can be reverted by restoring the original function. Assess whether that remaining uncertainty changes the design decision; distinguish a deferred check from a verified result.
evals.expected_output: The design is acceptable or has at most nonblocking advice. It eliminates repeated compilation using an explicit stateless-renderer contract, preserves the empty-input no-compile/no-error path and nonempty syntax errors, and avoids new global lifecycle ownership. The materiality of timing benefits remains unmeasured but has a feasible pre-merge check and a cheap local reversal, so lack of timing execution alone is not blocking. Planned checks are not observed passes. No requirement to first perform unrelated concurrency or system-wide E2E work should be invented.
assertions: Does not block solely because the performance timing comparison has not been executed, given the supported reuse contract, explicit pre-merge validation, and cheap reversal.
Grounds correctness in the stateless reusable renderer contract and recognizes that the empty-row guard preserves the original absence of compilation and syntax errors for empty input.
Separates established removal of repeated compilation from the unmeasured size of any timing benefit and does not claim planned comparisons passed.
Assesses the deferred assumption's impact, feasible timing check, and revert/abandon response without requiring a global cache, broader redesign, or unrelated validation.
Reviews the supplied proposal in review-only mode rather than replacing it with a newly generated design or implementing a repair.

evals.prompt: Use code-designer in supplied-design review-only mode. You are a fresh reviewer and did not author this proposal. Do not regenerate the design or edit code. Review this export-order design and proposed acceptance evidence before implementation planning. Give your actual blocking/advisory/none findings, evidence for the important claims, and the smallest corrections. User request/contract: CSV data rows must be oldest-to-newest by the instant at which an event occurred, regardless of the timestamp's timezone offset. Equal instants are ordered by ASCII event id. Preserve each row's original timestamp string in the CSV. All inputs are valid offset-bearing ISO timestamps. Existing exporter writes the input order unchanged. Proposal: copy the rows, sort by parsed epoch milliseconds and then by ASCII id, and give that ordered copy to the existing CSV writer; leave original rows and timestamp strings untouched. No new persistence or UI state. Proposed acceptance uses the public CSV-export entry point, decodes its output, and compares the row IDs and timestamp strings to a hand-authored oracle. Input rows: A has 2028-05-10T09:20:00+02:00; B has 2028-05-10T08:10:00Z; C has 2028-05-10T03:45:00-04:00. The oracle expects IDs [C, B, A], with their original timestamp strings, because 03:45 precedes 08:10 and 09:20. Another fixture uses equal instants with IDs b and a and expects [a, b]. There is no code yet and no check has run. Is the plan ready, and what, if anything, should change?
evals.expected_output: Identify a blocking acceptance-oracle error without incorrectly condemning the proposed instant-based sorting algorithm. A is 07:20Z, C is 07:45Z, and B is 08:10Z, so the correct public CSV order is [A, C, B]. The supplied [C, B, A] oracle ranks local clock strings, would reject a correct implementation, and could reward the wrong behavior. Correct the expected order using the contract, preserve original timestamp strings and the equal-instant ASCII tie test, and keep the artifact-level CSV observation. No wider redesign or timestamp normalization in the exported data is needed.
assertions: Identifies the proposed acceptance oracle as materially wrong for the required instant-based ordering rather than accepting it because it uses the public CSV boundary.
Independently derives the chronological order [A, C, B] from the offsets, with a correct explanation or equivalent UTC conversions.
Distinguishes the valid proposed sort-by-instant design from the incorrect expected outcome and recommends correcting the oracle rather than altering the algorithm to pass it.
Retains the original timestamp-string guarantee and meaningful equal-instant ASCII-id observation, without requiring transformed timestamps or an unrelated export redesign.
Reviews the supplied proposal in review-only mode rather than replacing it with a newly generated design or implementing a repair.
